item.title: Uniform Regulations and Rules for Bankers' Clearing Houses - Version 2.0 - November 2026
Procedural Guidelines for Cheque Truncation System - Version 3.0 - November 2026
Census on Foreign Liabilities and Assets of Indian Direct Investment Entities for 2025-26
item.description:
Today, the Reserve Bank released the provisional results of the 2025-261 round of the annual census on foreign liabilities and assets (FLA) covering cross-border liabilities and assets of the Indian entities [viz., companies, limited liability partnerships (LLPs), alternative investment funds (AIFs) and partnership firms] with inward/outward direct investment. The FLA census captures detailed information on foreign liabilities and assets in terms of direct investment, portfolio investment and other investments comprising of trade credit, loans, currency & deposits and other payables and receivables accounts, activity sector, sales, purchase, exports, and imports. The variations in outstanding foreign assets / liabilities between the beginning and end of a financial year would be different from flows recorded in India’s balance of payments (BoP) statistics during the year, as the former would also include valuation changes due to price and exchange rate movements.

Key highlights:

  • Of the total number of Indian entities reporting foreign direct investment (FDI) and/or overseas direct investment (ODI), around 97 per cent entities were unlisted as at end-March 2026, and also held a major share in total FDI equity capital (at face value) in India (Tables 1 and 2A).

  • Non-financial companies accounted for more than 90 per cent of the FDI equity at face value (Table 2B).

  • In terms of market value, listed and unlisted companies had almost equal share in total FDI equity capital as at end-March 2026, however, 96.6 per cent of the FDI debt is held by unlisted companies (Table 3A).

  • In rupee terms, the ratio of inward FDI to ODI moderated to 4.2 times as on end-March 2026 from 5.5 times a year ago (Table 3B).

  • Other investment liabilities [viz., trade credit, loans, currency and deposits, and other payables with unrelated (third party) non-resident entities] recorded a growth of 11.9 per cent (y-o-y) in rupee terms as on end-March 2026; other investment assets with unrelated non-residents also rose by 16.1 per cent during the same period (Table 4).

  • The United States of America (16.5 per cent) followed by Mauritius (14.5 per cent), Singapore (13.7 per cent) and the United Kingdom (10.8 per cent) were the top sources of outstanding FDI. In case of ODI, Singapore, the United Arab Emirates and the United States of America were the top destinations together accounting for more than 50 per cent share (Tables 5 and 6).

  • Manufacturing sector accounted for the highest share in the total outstanding FDI equity capital at market value (50.1 per cent), while 45 per cent share was held by services sector (Tables 7 and 8).

(Brij Raj)           
Chief General Manager

Press Release: 2026-2027/1463

item.title: Monetary and Credit Information Review
item.description:
Contents
Sections
I. Monetary Policy
II. Regulation
III. Central Board Meeting
IV. Surveys
V. Conference
VI. Publications
VII. Data Releases

Volume XXII | Issue 7 | October 2026
MONETARY & CREDIT INFORMATION REVIEW

Note from the Editor

This issue of the Monetary & Credit Information Review presents the Reserve Bank's principal policy and engagement events of the month. The Monetary Policy Committee, in its fourth bi-monthly meeting of 2026-27 held on October 5–7, 2026, unanimously increased the policy repo rate by 25 bps to 5.50 per cent, with the SDF rate at 5.25 per cent and the MSF rate and Bank Rate at 5.75 per cent, and changed the stance to calibrated tightening, as announced by Governor Shri Sanjay Malhotra on October 7, 2026. The 625th meeting of the Central Board, held at Chennai on October 30, 2026 under the Governor's chairmanship, deliberated on prevailing economic conditions, assessed risks to the outlook, and reviewed the working of DICGC and select Central Office Departments, with Deputy Governors and Directors in attendance. The 36th Conference of State Finance Secretaries, held at Mumbai on October 27, 2026 on the theme 'Role of Quality of Expenditure, Effective Cash and Prudent Debt Management in Enhancing States' Fiscal Sustainability', was inaugurated by the Governor, who urged States to maintain the quality of expenditure, adopt prudent borrowing and efficient cash management practices, onboard onto ULI, use P-CBDC for DBT and make effective use of the SLBC forum.

We remain committed to our goal of sharing accurate information and fostering deeper understanding. The MCIR can be accessed at https://mcir.rbi.org.in as well as by scanning the QR Code. We welcome your feedback at mcir@rbi.org.in.

Brij Raj
Editor

I. Monetary Policy

Governor’s Monetary Policy Statement on October 7, 2026

The sudden reescalation of the West Asia conflict in September and the consequent hardening and volatility in global crude prices soured global economic sentiments and heightened financial market volatility. Although global growth remains resilient, it is projected to decelerate in 2026 from the previous year. Driven by escalating energy costs and rising food prices, global inflation is projected to increase sharply prompting monetary policy tightening by major central banks. Lingering trade uncertainty, rising bond yields in advanced economies and an appreciating dollar are keeping global financial market sentiments nervous and fragile. Further tightening of global financial conditions, uncertainty about fair valuation of AI stocks, and an elusive resolution of the West Asia conflict pose significant downside risks to the global economic outlook.

In this global backdrop, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) met on 5th, 6th and 7th of this month to deliberate and decide on the policy repo rate. After a detailed assessment of the evolving macroeconomic and financial developments and the outlook, the MPC voted unanimously to increase the policy repo rate under the liquidity adjustment facility (LAF) by 25 bps to 5.50 per cent. Consequently, the standing deposit facility (SDF) rate stands adjusted at 5.25 per cent and the marginal standing facility (MSF) rate and the Bank Rate at 5.75 per cent. The MPC also decided to change the stance to calibrated tightening. I shall now briefly set out the rationale for these decisions.

The MPC noted that the global context on account of geopolitical developments remains challenging. Nonetheless, the Indian economy has been strong, and the economic momentum remains broad-based. Moreover, the economy is expected to remain resilient.

It further observed that in light of available data, it is clear that inflation and its outlook are not benign as they were last year, with headline CPI inflation expected to average almost 5.8 per cent in the next three quarters and core inflation projected at 4.4 per cent this financial year. In this milieu, recalibrating the policy rate is imperative.

As regards supply side inflation, the MPC noted that monetary policy primarily acts by curtailing second round effects (inflation expectations and firm level pricing behaviour, etc.), which take time to manifest and are difficult to extract from available data. Apart from data related to inflation expectations and firm level pricing behaviour, indicators of generalisation of inflation like core inflation and diffusion indices are used for this purpose. It may, however, be kept in mind that it is difficult to distinguish between the second-round effects and the indirect impact of supply side pressures (in production cost through energy and other inputs) as both are present in these indicators. While there is some evidence of elevated inflation expectations and generalisation of inflation, there are limited signs of supply side pressures getting embedded in pricing behaviour.

Similarly, while there is limited evidence of demand side pressures, risks in view of strong growth in monetary and credit aggregates exist.

Considering all these factors, the MPC unanimously voted to increase the policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent. The MPC also decided to change the stance to calibrated tightening. It underscored that given the current conditions, rate cuts are off the table in the near term and policy action ahead can only be a rate hike or a pause, depending on the evolving conditions and the outlook. The duration and extent of the rate hike cycle would be contingent on the actual growth-inflation developments and outlook, especially that of underlying inflation, the extent of broadening of price pressures and second round effects of the supply shock, as also the impact of demand impulses. To read the full statement, please click here.

Statement on Developmental and Regulatory Policies

Regulation

1. Measures to Enhance the Customer Convenience through the Account Aggregator Framework

With an objective to enhance customer convenience, it has been decided to implement interoperability among NBFC-Account Aggregators (NBFC-AA). This will enable customers to access and share their financial information, across different Financial Information Providers through any NBFC-AA of their choice. Additionally, Depositories regulated by the Securities and Exchange Board of India are being facilitated to include information related to bank deposit accounts in their Consolidated Account Statement (CAS) through the NBFC-AAs. This will enable demat account holders to view information relating to their demat account holdings and bank deposit accounts at one place in the CAS. Customers, including those who do not have demat accounts, can continue to obtain a consolidated view of their financial information and share the same through the NBFC - AAs also. Both measures aim to enhance customer convenience and are expected to be implemented by December 31, 2026.

Financial Markets

2. Constitution of a Technical Consultative Committee for Financial Markets

Against the backdrop of rapidly evolving financial markets and infrastructure, the Reserve Bank has decided to constitute a Technical Consultative Committee for Financial Markets. The Committee will serve as a forum for structured engagement with market participants and stakeholders by the Reserve Bank on policy and operational matters related to money, government securities and foreign exchange markets as well as the respective derivative markets and infrastructure. The composition and the terms of reference for the Technical Consultative Committee shall be separately notified.

Minutes of MPC

The 63rd Meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee, constituted under Section 45ZB of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, was held during October 5 to 7, 2026. Accordingly, under Section 45ZL of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, the Reserve Bank published the minutes of the proceedings of the meeting on October 21, 2026, i.e., the fourteenth day after meeting of the MPC. In the light of evolving developments on the global and domestic front, the MPC reviewed in detail the staff’s macroeconomic projections that included inputs from survey results and stakeholder consultations. The MPC also reviewed alternative scenarios around various risks to the outlook. Drawing on the above and after extensive discussions on the stance of monetary policy, the MPC adopted the resolution that is set out below. To read more, please click here.

II. Regulation

RBI issues Directions on 'Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Framework’

The Reserve Bank of India had issued draft Directions on the ‘Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Framework’ on August 7, 2026, inviting feedback from stakeholders until August 28, 2026. The draft Directions proposed modifications to the instructions on capital charge for CVA risk for commercial banks. Key revisions included: (i) allowing eligible banks to choose a simpler approach; (ii) increasing the sensitivity of supervisory risk weights for counterparties by sector and credit quality; (iii) clarifying the eligibility and recognition of CVA hedges; and (iv) separate systematic and idiosyncratic CVA risk components in the full Basic Approach (BA-CVA) calculation, addressing imperfect alignment of indirect CVA hedges. Feedback received on the draft instructions has been examined and consequent modifications have been suitably incorporated in the final Directions. Statement on the feedback received on the draft instructions is provided in the Annex. Accordingly, the Reserve Bank released the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Valuation Adjustment Framework) Directions, 2026 on October 7, 2026. These instructions will come into effect from April 1, 2027.

RBI issues guidelines on the implementation of Leverage Ratio 2017 Standard

The Reserve Bank of India had issued the draft Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Eleventh Amendment Directions, 2026 on August 7, 2026, inviting feedback from stakeholders until August 28, 2026. The draft Amendment Directions proposed to implement the latest leverage ratio framework ('Leverage Ratio 2017 Standard') issued by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision. Feedback received on the draft Directions has been examined and consequent modifications have been suitably incorporated in the final Amendment Directions. The statement on the feedback received on the draft Directions is provided in the Annex. Accordingly, the Reserve Bank released the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Eleventh Amendment Directions, 2026 on October 23, 2026. These instructions will come into effect from April 1, 2027.

RBI issues Amendment Directions on 'Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR)’

The Reserve Bank of India had issued draft Amendment Directions on the ‘Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR)’ on June 10, 2026, inviting feedback from stakeholders until July 1, 2026. The draft Amendment Directions proposed modifications to the instructions on capital charge for counterparty credit risk as provided in Master Direction on Forthcoming Instructions for commercial banks. Key revisions included: (i) clarifying the scope of CCR for both banking and trading book exposures, (ii) addressing treatment of multiple margin agreements and multiple netting sets in light of recent legal / regulatory developments, (iii) providing guidance for transactions where a bank acts as a clearing member of SEBI-recognised stock exchanges in the equity derivatives and commodity derivatives segments, (iv) specifying the treatment for deferment of option premium, (v) offering guidance on computing effective notional for options, and (vi) including disclosure templates for SA-CCR. Feedback received on the draft instructions has been examined and consequent modifications have been suitably incorporated in the final Amendment Directions. Statement on the feedback received on the draft instructions is provided in the Annex. Accordingly, the Reserve Bank released the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions) Amendment Directions, 2026 on October 7, 2026. These instructions will come into effect from April 1, 2027.

III. 625th Meeting of Central Board of the Reserve Bank of India

The 625th Meeting of the Central Board of Directors of Reserve Bank of India was held on October 30, 2026, in Mumbai under the Chairmanship of Shri Sanjay Malhotra, Governor. The Central Board took the Integrity Pledge as part of the observance of Vigilance Awareness Week 2026.

The Board in its meeting deliberated on the prevailing economic conditions and associated challenges and evaluated the potential risks to the economic outlook. The Board reviewed the activities of Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation and activities of select Central Office Departments of the Bank.

Deputy Governors, Shri Swaminathan J., Dr. Poonam Gupta, Shri Shirish Chandra Murmu, Shri Rohit Jain, and other Directors of the Central Board, viz., Ms. Anuradha Thakur, Secretary, Department of Economic Affairs; Shri Anand Gopal Mahindra, Shri Janmejaya Kumar Sinha, Shri Syed Akbaruddin and Ms. Annie George Mathew attended the meeting.

RBI issues Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions) Second Amendment Directions, 2026 on Minimum Capital Requirements for Operational Risk

The Reserve Bank of India had issued Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions) Directions, 2025 on November 28, 2025. Chapter IV of these Directions prescribed the Minimum Capital Requirements for Operational Risk, wherein it was specified that the effective date of implementation and indicative mapping of the components of the Business Indicator (BI) to the schedules and line items of the financial statements shall be provided in due course. Subsequently, Governor in his Statement dated October 01, 2025, announced that the revised Basel III capital adequacy framework for Commercial Banks (excluding Small Finance Banks (SFBs), Payment Banks (PBs), Regional Rural Banks(RRBs)) would come into effect from April 01, 2027. Further, post issuance of these Directions, certain additional clarifications have been issued by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision. In view of the above developments, the Reserve Bank released the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions) Second Amendment Directions, 2026 on October 23, 2026 specifying the implementation date for the new Standardised Approach (‘Basel III Standardised Approach’ or ‘Basel III SA’) for minimum operational risk regulatory capital requirements, providing an indicative mapping of BI components, and incorporating additional clarifications.

IV. Surveys

RBI launches Quarterly Order Books, Inventories and Capacity Utilisation Survey: July – September 2026

The Reserve Bank of India has launched the 75th round of its Order Books, Inventories and Capacity Utilisation Survey (OBICUS). The survey is for the reference period July – September 2026 (Q2:2026-27). The Reserve Bank has been conducting the Order Books, Inventories and Capacity Utilisation Survey (OBICUS) of the manufacturing sector on a quarterly basis since 2008. The information collected in the survey includes quantitative data on new orders received during the reference quarter, backlog of orders at the beginning of the quarter, pending orders at the end of the quarter, total inventories with a breakup between ﬁnished goods (FG), work-in-progress (WiP) and raw material (RM) inventories at the end of the quarter, item-wise production in terms of quantity and value during the quarter vis-à-vis the installed capacity from the targeted group and the reasons for changes in production / installed capacity during the quarter. The level of capacity utilisation (CU) is estimated from these responses. The survey provides valuable input for monetary policy formulation. The survey findings are released on the website of the Bank regularly. To read more, please click here.

Launching of 51st Round of Quarterly Services and Infrastructure Outlook Survey (SIOS) Q3:2026-27

The Reserve Bank has launched the 51st round of the quarterly Services and Infrastructure Outlook Survey (SIOS) for the reference period October-December 2026. The survey assesses the business situation for the current quarter (Q3:2026-27) from selected companies in the services and infrastructure sectors in India and their expectations for the ensuing quarter (Q4:2026-27) based on qualitative responses on a set of indicators pertaining to demand conditions, financial conditions, employment conditions and the price situation. The outlook on key parameters for the two subsequent quarters (Q1:2027-28 and Q2:2027-28) are also covered. To read more, please click here.

Launching of 116th Round of Quarterly Industrial Outlook Survey (IOS) - Q3:2026-27

The Reserve Bank has launched the 116th round of the quarterly Industrial Outlook Survey (IOS) of the Indian manufacturing sector for the reference period October-December 2026. The survey assesses business sentiments for the current quarter (Q3:2026-27) and expectations for the ensuing quarter (Q4:2026-27), based on qualitative responses on a set of indicators pertaining to demand conditions, financial conditions, employment conditions and the price situation. The outlook on key parameters for the two subsequent quarters (Q1:2027-28 and Q2:2027-28) are also covered. The survey findings are released in summary form on the website of the Bank regularly, where identity of the respondents is not revealed. To read more, please click here.

V. Reserve Bank holds 36th Conference of State Finance Secretaries

The 36th Conference of State Finance Secretaries was held on October 27, 2026 at RBI, Mumbai. The theme of the Conference was ‘Role of Quality of Expenditure, Effective Cash and Prudent Debt Management in Enhancing States’ Fiscal Sustainability’. The Conference was attended by the Finance Secretaries of 27 States and three Union Territories as well as senior officials from the Ministry of Finance, Government of India, Controller General of Accounts and the Comptroller and Auditor General of India. Governor, Reserve Bank of India inaugurated the Conference.

Addressing the participants, the Governor emphasised the importance of maintaining the quality of expenditure to ensure the long-term fiscal health of the States. He also emphasised on the need for the States to adopt prudent borrowing strategies and efficient cash management practices. The Governor urged the States to onboard onto the Unified Lending Interface (ULI) and utilise Programmable Central Bank Digital Currency (P-CBDC) for Direct Benefit Transfers (DBT). He also advised States to make effective use of the State Level Bankers’ Committee (SLBC) forum. During the Conference, the Governor released a Booklet titled ‘Compendium on Cash and Debt Management for State Governments’. The Booklet summarises relevant concepts, operational processes and good cash and debt management practices in a concise and accessible format.

The meeting reviewed, inter alia, market borrowings by the States, short-term financial accommodation to the States from Reserve Bank, adoption of Benchmark Issuance Strategy by the States, etc.

VI. Publications

RBI Bulletin – October 2026

The Reserve Bank released the October 2026 issue of its monthly Bulletin on October 23, 2026. The Bulletin includes two speeches, four articles and current statistics.

The four articles are:

I. State of the Economy

Renewed geopolitical frictions in West Asia and supply chain disruptions have amplified inflationary pressures, prompting major central banks to raise policy rates. Elevated sovereign bond yields in advanced economies (AEs) have also brought into focus concerns about fiscal sustainability and its implications for financial stability. The Indian economy continued to demonstrate strength as evidenced by high-frequency indicators across both industry and services.

II. Transmission to Lending Rates of SCBs: Price versus Composition Effects in WALR

This article analyses the transmission of monetary policy to the fresh lending rates of scheduled commercial banks by decomposing variations in the weighted average lending rate (WALR) into interest rate effects and compositional effects. Using an index-number based framework on bank and sector level lending rates and loan weights, the study examines the extent to which changes in the aggregate WALR reflect changes in lending rates and shifts in credit composition.

III. Performance of the NBFC Sector: Review for 2025

This article assesses the performance of the non-banking financial company (NBFC) sector up to end-December 2025. It also provides a bird’s-eye-view of India’s financial system. Employing a text-mining approach, the article also explores the extent and nature of orientation towards artificial intelligence (AI) by select NBFCs.

IV. Nowcasting State-Level Economic Activity in India with Night-Time Light and Google Trends

Timely measurement of state-level economic activity remains a challenge in India, as official Gross State Value Added (GSVA) data are released annually with a considerable lag. This study demonstrates how alternative data sources, specifically satellite-based night-time lights and digital search behaviour, can be used to generate high-frequency estimates of state-level economic activity. The framework is applied to three major states — Maharashtra, Karnataka and Gujarat. To read more, please click here.

VII. Data Releases

Important data released by the Reserve Bank during the month of October 2026 are as follows:

S/N Title
1 RBI releases the results of Forward Looking Surveys
2 Scheduled Banks’ Statement of Position in India as on October 15, 2026
3 Lending and Deposit Rates of Scheduled Commercial Banks – October 2026
4 Sectoral Deployment of Bank Credit – September 2026
5 Monthly Data on India’s International Trade in Services for the Month of September 2026

item.title: RBI WPS (DEPR): 01/2026: Data Gaps in State-Level Inflation: An Assessment for the Covid Period
item.description:
Press Release

RBI Working Paper Series No. 01

Data Gaps in State-Level Inflation: An Assessment for the Covid Period

Purnima Shaw and R. K. Sinha@

Abstract

1 The disruption during Covid-19 necessitated statistical organisations across the world to impute the missing official statistics data or explore alternative data sources. The Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI’s) Inflation Expectations Survey of Households (IESH) continued to be conducted (using telephonic interviews) during the pandemic months. While imputed figures for the official price indices are available at the aggregate level for April and May 2020, the State-wise inflation data remains unpublished (missing) for four of the pandemic months. This paper uses granular IESH data and takes a distributional approach to provide State-wise inflation estimates for these data gaps. These State-wise inflation estimates when aggregated, closely follow the all-India official CPI inflation series.

JEL Classification: D84, E17, E31

Keywords: Consumer price index, distribution function, inflation, inflation expectations

Introduction

The outbreak of the coronavirus (Covid-19) pandemic across the globe and the related administrative measures implemented to control its spread, e.g., closure of non-essential businesses, public offices and restricted movements resulted in a severe disturbance in the routine compilation and dissemination of official statistics. In such a scenario, the compilers of official statistics, like Central Banks and National Statistical Offices across the world needed to retain the confidence of the users of official statistics in the data. The need of the hour was to ensure complete transparency in the data collection and dissemination processes. A possible way forward was to make concerted efforts to collect the required data, drawing on both current and alternative sources, to compile reliable statistics and cover data gaps using universally accepted methodologies. Statisticians in various data compiling positions, were proactive in handling these challenges and exploring new ways to address the gaps in collection of data. The challenges in the compilation of the Consumer Price Indices (CPI) were profound. During the Covid period of restricted movement, limited shops were operational, and several consumer items were unavailable in shops because of supply chain issues. In addition, restrictions on physical movement made data collection for the limited available items largely unfeasible. Further, the ability to conduct surveys was also impacted severely.

Statisticians around the world had to adapt to these data compilation challenges and adopt various methodologies available in the literature for addressing missing data. To fill-in the missing information, data imputation was followed mostly across the economies. In spite of these, several challenges were being faced by the data users including Central Banks across the world in analysing these imputed official statistics which included uncertainty in the imputed figures; changes in the consumption basket due to pandemic related supply constraints resulting in biased price deflators; delay in data dissemination; frequent revisions in data and its composition; changes in data collection methodology; varying seasonal patterns in data; uncertainty in data biases (e.g., time variation, impact of the changing economy and policy actions); sample representativeness due to limited access; outdated profile of survey respondents; changes in time series trends leading to the risk of increasing bias in estimates; reduced response rates with less accurate responses due to pandemic-related priorities; and constraints related to auxiliary data sharing because of limited resources and delays due to the pandemic (Beer and Tissot, 2021).

To address the need for analysing timely data during the pandemic induced uncertainties, Central Banks required high frequency data from alternative sources in place of the traditional sources (Hinge, 2020). High frequency data sources were used to decipher the dynamics of important macroeconomic conditions. The use of such high frequency data in this regard were proved to be useful in studies by Hopkins and Sherman (2020) for Ireland, Bank of Japan (2020), Davies et al. (2020) for Bank of England and Chapman and Desai (2021) for Canada. However, these high frequency data have their own limitations as they need to be adjusted for seasonality, weather conditions, and other relevant factors (Castelletti et al., 2020 and Beer and Tissot, 2021). Further, innovative methods needed to be quickly explored for dealing with the methodological issues induced by the range of vast policy measures being taken by administrative authorities in response to the pandemic. Beer and Tissot (2021) suggested better use of existing big data sources, taking advantage of the progressing digital innovation for building automated link within granular datasets. In spite of all these efforts, certain gaps remain in official statistics during the pandemic period, resulting in a break in the time series data.

While data on several commodity prices were imputed across economies, including India, there remain certain data gaps during the pandemic period, due to insufficient data collection. In case of India, imputed price indices for the official inflation were released at the aggregate level for the months of April and May 2020. However, the State-wise official inflation figures are missing for four of the pandemic months. Taking cues from Shaw and Sinha (2024) which highlights the importance of the granular dataset on the RBI’s IESH in nowcasting and forecasting State-wise inflation figures, and adaptive nature of the households’ inflation expectations in India, the current paper makes a novel attempt of using households’ inflation perceptions and expectations to present urban inflation estimates for the States for the pandemic months of April and May, 2020 and 2021.

Section II of the paper reviews various data imputation techniques from the existing literature followed by cross country estimates and use of alternative data for imputation. Section III explains the proposed methodology for estimating the missing State-wise urban inflation data. The first part of Section IV examines the performance of the proposed methodology using existing data and then proposes State-wise estimates for the months of April and May 2020 and 2021. This is followed by the concluding remarks in Section V.

II. Estimation of Missing Time-Series Data

Missing data may arise due to a random mechanism or a structural deficiency. The structural deficiency indicates that a component of data is omitted. Random missing mechanism can be classified into three categories as follows (Kuhn and Johnson, 2020):

i. Missing Completely at Random (MCAR): The missing data is due to a random mechanism and the probability of missingness is same for the existing as well as missing data. An example of this could be missing price data due to the closure of a shop with significant business profile.

ii. Missing at Random (MAR): The probability of missingness is not the same for the existing and missing data and it depends on the existing data and not on the missing data. Observed data can be used to predict the missing data. For example, missing data on quarterly gross domestic product (GDP) of a financial year can be approximated with the help of available annual GDP estimate and past quarterly GDP estimates.

iii. Not Missing at Random (NMAR): The missing data is related to the non-observed data. The missingness is due to the factors which are not considered during data collection. For example, data on sensitive economic variables like individual income, savings, etc.

The missing CPI data during Covid period can be classified as Missing Completely at Random (MCAR). If the missing mechanism is MCAR and the loss is low, then ignoring/ deleting the missing data can be a feasible option (Ribeiro and Castro, 2022). However, the loss in this case is significant and cannot be afforded, as deletion will result in a break in time series, thereby impacting the entire forecasting process and analysis. Hence, data imputation becomes necessary for estimating the missing CPI data for the pandemic period.

A few imputation techniques following Pratama et al. (2016), Ribeiro and Castro (2022) and Rocha et al. (2024), are mean, median and mode imputation which replace the missing data with mean, median or mode of the remaining features (other related variables) of the data. This is suitable for stationary time series data; hot deck imputation which searches for data on features like those related to the sample on missing data and replace the missing data with a random data from the similar sets (Andridge and Little, 2010); cold deck imputation which replaces the missing data with a random data from the similar sets from a different data source (Duma et al., 2013); forward and backward filling which replaces missing data with the last observed data (forward filling) or with the next observed data (backward filling) under the assumption that missing data is similar to the adjacent data points (Molnar et al., 2008). However, this method creates an issue if there is seasonality in the variable.

Other techniques include multiple imputation which calculates multiple imputed values with a probability distribution for a missing data. These data are examined and combined to generate realistic estimate (Azur et al., 2011). The method is suitable for imputing missing data in survey with MAR mechanism. Linear interpolation techniques have been used to compute using a linear function to connect the nearest points to represent the data well while spline interpolation has been used for computing missing values using a polynomial function to connect the nearest points to represent the data well (Elissavet, 2017). Holt’s (1957) exponential weighted moving average can also be used wherein, the imputed figure is derived as a weighted average of the historical data points. The weighting factors reduce exponentially for the older time points. Fix and Hodges’ (1951) k-nearest neighbour method is appropriate when the distribution of the data is unknown. The method uses the average or median of the target values from the k nearest neighbours to make a prediction of the missing value. Kalman prediction (pioneered by Swerling, 1958, Kalman, 1960 and Kalman and Bucy, 1961) is a linear model of estimation based on an algorithm and consists of two processes: a prediction stage and a correction stage. In missing indicators method, for each of the partially observed feature, a corresponding indicator variable is added to indicate the missingness using binary values. It can be used with any imputation method, but is most commonly used with mean imputation (Groenwold et al., 2012). Expectation maximisation method uses other features to impute the missing value and then checks whether it is the most probable value. This step is iterated till the most probable value is found (Dempster et al., 1977). Other recent imputation methods include ST-2SMR (Cheng and Lu, 2017), temporal belief memory (Kim and Chi, 2018), long short-term memory (Patterson and Gibson, 2017) and generative adversarial imputation network (Yoon et al., 2018).

II.1. Cross Country Experiences

Cross-country experiences show a wide-range of techniques that were used by various economies to fill-up the gap in commodity prices during Covid-19 period. The Office for National Statistics in the U.K. imputed2 the prices of items which were either unavailable or available in a limited manner. The imputation was based on the method that best reflected the price behaviour of the missing commodity. The imputations were based on three methods: first, using the price index immediately above the item in classification structure; second, using the price movement of a similar commodity; and third, applying forward filling. For imputing a missing price of non-seasonal commodities, combined monthly growth of all available non-imputed commodity prices was used.

The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics imputed missing prices using cell-relative imputation method3. In this method, imputed price is derived using the average price change of all items similar to the missing item in one month for the same geographic area. This method is used for commodities where it may be safely assumed that the price changes in the missing items would be similar to the price changes in the other items. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics listed down items for which data was inadequate for publication during each of the pandemic months.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics used three types of imputation4 techniques. For available goods and services, for which prices were temporarily unavailable, imputed price was taken as the average price change of similar goods and services. For unavailable goods and services, where a significant amount of its typical expenditure has been substituted to another good or service, donor imputation technique was used, wherein price change of a donor commodity is considered. For unavailable goods and services, where expenditure cannot be substituted by any other commodity, prices were imputed off the headline CPI.

The Department: Statistics South Africa (Stats SA) practiced two types of imputation techniques5. The price change of commodities for which no expenditure was possible due to the restricted movement, imputed prices were taken as the change in the headline CPI index of all items based on those products, for which prices were either available or imputed by other methods. For the items which are either quarterly or annually collected, the previous month’s corresponding indices were carried forward. The price change in diesel was imputed using the change in the regulated wholesale price of diesel. Certain items under the personal care group were possibly available for sale, but their prices could not be collected, and therefore, were imputed by the personal care index.

In India, the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MOSPI) imputed6 the prices of sub-groups under the food group by multiplying the last observed index of the sub-group with the price relative of food group index calculated based on the available prices. Imputation of the prices of sub-groups under the non-food group were done by multiplying the last observed index of the sub-group with the price relative of general CPI index calculated based on the available prices.

Despite extensive use of imputation techniques in presenting missing CPI values during the pandemic period, there exists missing data in the CPI in India. During the months of April and May 2020, the complete CPI State-wise data could not be collected due to the restrictions imposed to curb the spread of Covid-19. The MOSPI released the CPI provisional indices for select groups and sub-groups for the months of April and May 2020 on the 12th day of May and June, 20207 respectively. These releases stated that the general indices and State-wise indices could not be compiled. Later, on July 13, 2020, a technical note8 was released which contained imputed general indices for both the months. However, the State-wise estimates could not be constructed as the number of price quotations received (through both telephonic conversations and physical visits to neighbourhood shops) was insufficient. In the year 2021, State-wise indices were released for both the months of April and May, but the inflation could not be compiled due to the absence of the indices in the corresponding months in 2020. As a result, there remains a break in the State-wise inflation series for the months of April and May during the years 2020 and 2021. The blank cells in Table 1 show the existing gaps in the CPI data. The cells highlighted in green represent the gaps, which this paper attempts to fill-in.

II.2. Use of Alternative Data Sources for Imputation

Apart from the above-mentioned methodologies on imputation, there have been attempts of estimating the missing data by making use of alternative data sources. Cavallo (2020) used the credit and debit card transactions between the first five months of 2020 and presented inflation estimates for the U.S. economy. These were found to be higher than the official inflation. The gap ranges from 0.1 percentage points in March 2020 to 0.7 percentage points in April 2020 followed by 0.8 in May 2020. Based on bank card transactions, Gautier et al. (2023) calculated similar estimates for France from January to December 2020. Their estimates were also on the higher side with the largest gap being 1.1 percentage points in April 2020. Using debit card data, Jonckheere and Zimmer (2020) presented such revised estimates for Belgium from February to July 2020. The estimates were on the higher side than the official inflation from March 2020 to July 2020.

Kouvavas et al. (2020) used aggregate turnover data to estimate the changing consumption patterns and derived revised inflation figures for the Euro area from January to August 2020. With a finding similar to the above-mentioned ones, the gap between the estimates and the official inflation peaked to 0.25 percentage points in May 2020. The findings of Huynh et al. (2020) indicate marginal uptick in the estimated inflation obtained using high frequency expenditure network data (on debit card purchases) from the official inflation during March, April and May 2020 in Canada. The differences are 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 percentage points, respectively.

Taking cue from these literatures which have used alternative data sources to estimate the inflation of the missing data during the Covid period, this paper attempts to make use of an alternative dataset in case of India, i.e., the RBI’s IESH granular data to derive estimates for the missing data in the State-wise CPI inflation. A recent study by Shaw and Sinha (2024) used the granular IESH data to nowcast and forecast the State-wise inflation figures. The current paper makes a novel attempt of using this data to present urban inflation estimates for the States for the pandemic months of April and May, 2020 and 2021, for which the CPI inflation data are missing.

III. Methodology

The use of alternative data sources in computing estimates of the unobservable economic variables during the pandemic period has been discussed in Section II. Alternative data may provide only limited information during normal periods of the economic cycle. However, such data are more indicative of the situation during crisis periods, more so for the short term (INSEE, 2020). RBI’s IESH data related to inflationary sentiments may be considered as an alternative dataset and hence, it has been used extensively in this paper9. The RBI’s Survey of Professional Forecasters (SPF) is also a rich dataset on all-India inflation forecasts; it cannot be used to study State-wise inflation estimates.

This paper attempts to fill-in the missing data on State-wise inflation for April and May, 2020 and 2021. State-wise inflation data are particularly important for studying State-specific information like inter-State transportation costs, State taxes, differences in States for supply chain management, etc., all of which contribute to the inflation volatility amongst States. The centre-wise survey data are also important for the study as various factors like respondents’ age, gender, occupation, location, etc., impact the sentiments of survey respondents rendering variability in the sentiments among various centres. Accordingly, the availability of estimates for the State-wise inflation for the specific months, which remains unpublished, would be potentially useful for any relevant study involving State-level inflation time-series data going forward, as the proposed estimates attempt to resolve the break in State-wise inflation series, to an extent.

During the Covid-19 pandemic and amid the ensuing restrictions, IESH managed a full-sample response by switching to either fully telephonic or a combination of telephonic and physical interviews during the rounds of May 202010, July 202011, September 202012, November 202013, January 202114, May 202115, July 202116 and September 202117. Taking cue from the adaptive nature of the households’ inflation expectations in India (Sharma and Bicchal, 2018, Shaw, 2019, Singh et al., 2024, Shaw, 2024, to name a few), RBI’s IESH18 may be considered as an alternative data to make a plausible conjecture about the State-wise inflation dynamics during April and May, 2020 and 2021, when inflation was volatile due to the disturbances in the demand-supply dynamics.

Recently, Shaw and Sinha (2024) attempted a novel method of mapping distributions of the centre-wise granular IESH data from the survey to the State-wise granular CPI-urban (CPI-U) inflation data to present State-level CPI-U inflation nowcasts and forecasts. Further, it is reasonable to expect that the demand-supply shocks due to the unprecedented pandemic must have impacted the CPI inflation as well as the households’ sentiments (Chart 1), making the latter even more relevant to use for the purpose. This section proposes a methodology for arriving at the inflation estimates of the urban19 areas of the States in which IESH is conducted for the months of April and May for the years 2020 and 2021. The exercise will be able to present urban inflation estimates for select States in the highlighted cells in Table 1.

The responses on inflation perceptions and expectations are collected in buckets of (<1%,1−<2%,…,15−<16%,≥16%). The respondents with inflation perception/ expectation beyond 15 per cent are requested to provide the exact inflation number. General characteristics of the data include the respondents’ preferences in polling their inflation perceptions and inflation expectations in multiples of five (Chart 2) (Sinha, 2023 and Shaw and Sinha, 2024). This makes the data distribution uneven and adds to the variation across the survey centres. Looking at the sample frequency distribution of inflation perceptions/ expectations of each of the survey centres for each of the study periods, the distribution can be smoothened by removing the sudden frequency spikes due to digit preference and by replacing such frequencies with approximate values obtained using interpolation method20. Here, the frequencies at multiples of 5 are assumed to be unknown and interpolated using the nearby frequencies. Let fi be the frequency for the ith response class. Let x be a continuous variable indicating responses and f(x) be a function of x representing the corresponding frequencies. Consider n values of f(x) are known and assume that f(x) is a polynomial of (n − 1) degrees,





respectively. Thus, the frequencies at multiples of 5 are replaced with positive interpolated frequencies, which make the sample frequency distribution smoother than the previous one. The properties (moments) of the smoothed distribution will not be like the true frequency distribution (captured in the survey) because the peaked frequencies at multiples of 5 observed due to respondents’ digit preference are averaged out. It appears that by doing so, there is information loss, but this is undertaken so that a workable and standard probability distribution can be fitted to the survey data. Shaw and Sinha (2024) have used the residual data (peaked frequencies) to nowcast and forecast the CPI inflation. These modified sample distributions are then fitted with various continuous probability distributions, viz., Normal, Laplace, Log-normal, Gamma, Logistic, Weibull and Log-logistic distributions and among these, an appropriate distribution is selected for fitting using the non-parametric Kolmogorov-Smirnov’s test for goodness of fit. Let g(x) be the fitted distribution.

Considering the distribution of the official CPI-U inflation (of eight months21 previous to the survey month) of each of the 17 States, where IESH is conducted for each of the 47 survey rounds, there are 799 distributions. These sample distributions are also fitted with the aforementioned seven probability distributions and an appropriate distribution is selected and fitted using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov’s test. Let h(y) be the fitted distribution and F(y) be the cumulative distribution function such that, for any real number “a”,

Corresponding to the probabilities g(x), the percentiles of F(a) can be tabulated using,

Using this derived distribution, the modal value from the distribution is taken as the inflation nowcast/ forecast. The nowcasts/ forecasts, thus derived, may be considered as the inflation estimates for the months for which CPI-U inflation data is missing.

IV. Numerical Illustration

Before moving on to fill-in the State-wise inflation data gap, it is necessary to apply the estimation techniques to the periods, for which the official inflation data are available. This will facilitate in gauging the quantum of error in the estimates using the methodology described in the previous section. For this purpose, centre-wise inflation perceptions and three-months ahead inflation expectations are considered from the IESH data for the 47 survey rounds during September 2016 to May 2024. One year ahead inflation expectations of consumers are not considered with the logic that such expectations would likely reflect outdated information in a rapidly evolving economic environment. The objective is to first examine the performance of inflation nowcasts using consumers’ inflation perceptions. Thereafter, the performance of three-months inflation forecasts, which were computed using consumers’ three-months ahead inflation expectations are to be testified. Given a survey centre for each of the 47 survey rounds above, corresponding State’s official CPI-U data for the previous eight months are taken as the reference data. For example, if it is required to nowcast CPI-U inflation of Gujarat for May 2024, then the survey data of Ahmedabad for the round May 2024 and CPI-U inflation data of Gujarat for the months September 2023 to April 2024 are considered. Further, for three months ahead forecast, in order to forecast the CPI-U inflation of Gujarat for April 2024, the survey data of Ahmedabad for the survey round January 2024 and CPI-U inflation data of Gujarat for the months May 2023 to December 2023 are considered.

There are 18 urban survey centres in the IESH data22, which are assumed to represent the urban areas of the respective 17 CPI States23. Considering the sample distribution of inflation perceptions/ expectations of each of the 18 survey centres for each of the 47 survey rounds, there are 846 distributions. A city-wise distribution of the responses (including exact responses beyond 15 per cent) for the study period in Chart 2 reflects the concentration of responses in multiples of 5, indicating the digit preference of respondents in polling inflation perceptions/ expectations. The intensity is, however, dying out with the increase in numbers. The responses are henceforth considered up to 20 per cent, representing about 92 per cent (89 per cent) of the inflation perceptions (three months ahead inflation expectations). The interpolated frequencies are obtained for frequencies at 5−<6%, 10−<11%, 15−<16% and 20% using equations 7 to 22.

Following the methodology described in Section III, the nowcasts and three months ahead inflation forecasts are obtained, and their performances with respect to the official CPI-U inflation figures (published by MOSPI), are gauged using the standard measures defined below:

where,

FEt = Ft - At
Ft = forecast for time periodt
At = actual at time periodt
T = number of time periods

A graphical view of the nowcasts and forecasts are presented in Charts 3 and 4. In Charts 4a and b, the nowcasts and forecasts are compared with the officially published CPI-U inflation aggregated for the survey states. It may be noted that a portion of the errors in nowcasts/ forecasts obtained using the proposed methodology can be attributed to the following assumptions:

i. Assumption of centres’ sentiments (with limited survey sample size) as the States’ sentiments.

ii. Inflation expectations are households’ own sentiments and cannot be linked to the CPI consumption baskets.


State-wise estimates for the missing months of April 2020 and April 2021 are the three months ahead CPI-U inflation forecasts for these months. Similarly, estimates for the missing months of May 2020 and May 2021 are the CPI-U inflation nowcasts for these months. Although, the nowcasts are better than the three months ahead forecasts in terms of reduced errors for April 2020 and April 2021, three months ahead forecasts are considered because nowcasts cannot be derived due to the absence of survey rounds in the month of April. The estimates are provided in Annex Tables A1 and A2.

Official CPI-U inflation figures of all-India are plotted along with the official CPI-U inflation aggregated figures of all survey States with the missing data for the months April and May 2020 and 2021 in the latter series being replaced with the respective nowcasts and forecasts (Chart 5). While the official CPI-U inflation figures for all-India and all survey States combined are close and differ only in decimals, the estimates of the latter for April 2020 and April 2021 appear to have not captured the true direction and additionally contain high error. This is not surprising because consumers are not expected to forecast the pandemic impact for April 2020 while they were responding for the January 2020 survey round. Further, forecast errors were found to be high just before the onset of Covid-19, i.e., during the two months before April 2020 (Chart 4). This may be attributed mainly due to the shock from the food group (particularly vegetables) in the last three quarters of 2019-20. The error in the estimates of April 2021 appears to be an impact of base effect from the April 2020 estimate. Comparatively, the estimate for May 2020 seems much less erroneous. On the other hand, the estimate for May 2021 seems to be somewhat higher.



Such refinement of estimates could be made possible only due to the availability of State-wise CPI-U price indices for April and May 2021 and all-India CPI-U inflation for all the four months of April and May 2020 and 2021. The revised estimates for the four months are provided in Annex Tables A3 and A4. State-wise CPI-U inflation figures with refined estimates in the vacant points are plotted in Annex Chart A1.

The refined estimates indicate improved performance as they closely follow the all-survey States’ combined CPI-U inflation and the published official all-India inflation (Chart 6). In the light of the low difference between the all-survey states combined inflation and all-India inflation, it may be safe to take the differences between the all-survey centres’ combined CPI-U inflation refined estimates and all-India inflation figures for April and May 2020 and 2021 as the forecast errors which indicates a forecast error in the range of -14 to 13 basis points in the inflation estimates of the missing months (Table 4).

Summing up, the objective was to fill-up the data gaps in the State-wise CPI-U inflation series during the months of April and May 2020 and 2021, owing to the Covid-19 pandemic related restrictions. Using centre-wise urban consumers’ inflation perceptions, three months ahead inflation expectations and past state-wise realised CPI-U inflation figures, State-wise inflation nowcasts and forecasts were calculated, and their performances were studied for a fairly long period. It was found that performance of the proposed State-wise inflation estimates with respect to the published State-wise MOSPI data of CPI-U inflation figures were comparable. Accordingly, the State-wise inflation nowcasts and forecasts were obtained for the months of April and May 2020 and 2021. These estimates were refined using the past error history adjusting for any error in the State-wise estimates due to sudden onset of the pandemic and its grossly unknown cascading impact on inflation. As the forecast error is low compared with alternative estimation forecasts like the interpolation method, the refined estimates provide a better measure to fill the data gaps during the Covid period.

V. Conclusion

The collection and compilation of official statistics suffered acutely during the outbreak of the Covid-19 pandemic due to the resulting restrictions across the world. In an environment of uncertainty, scarcity of data made it difficult to clearly understand the prevailing economic scenario. To address this issue and to retain the confidence of statisticians and economists in official statistics, statistical organisations attempted to impute the missing data. In India, State-wise CPI indices could not be collected on a full-fledged basis during the pandemic months of April and May 2020. As a result, State-wise CPI inflation figures are unavailable for the months of April and May 2020 and April and May 2021. In this context, this paper uses IESH granular data to derive State-wise CPI-U inflation estimates for these four pandemic months. These State-wise inflation estimates are of critical use in the current inflation targeting regime. Further, these also attempt to resolve the gap in the State-wise inflation series to an extent. When the State-wise inflation estimates are aggregated, the figures closely follow the all-India CPI inflation series published by MOSPI. Accordingly, State-wise inflation estimates for the specific months derived in this paper help in bridging the data gaps. These estimates are expected to be potentially useful for any relevant study. In future, these State-wise inflation estimates may be compared with model-based forecasts. The use of non-parametric methods may also be potentially explored to examine the scope of improvement in the proposed estimates.
