Foreword

The Monthly Bulletin of the Reserve Bank of India presents a structured compilation of key macroeconomic and financial statistics relating to the Indian economy. Over time, the scope, coverage, and presentation of these statistics have evolved in response to changes in the economic environment, statistical standards, and data dissemination practices.

This Handbook provides an updated and comprehensive guide to the concepts, definitions, classification principles and compilation frameworks underlying the tables published in the Current Statistics section of the RBI Bulletin. The objective of this Handbook is to promote consistency in interpretation and facilitate informed use of data by researchers, market participants, policy analysts, and the wider public.

It is expected that this Handbook will serve as a useful reference for users seeking clarity on data coverage, methodological conventions, and statistical relationships presented in the Bulletin. This edition supersedes the earlier version released in 2017.

(A R Joshi)
Executive Director
Department of Statistics and Information Management
Reserve Bank of India
April 2026

Preparation and Publication

This Handbook has been prepared by the Data Management and Dissemination Division (DMDD), Department of Statistics and Information Management (DSIM), Reserve Bank of India.

This Handbook is available on the Database on Indian Economy (DBIE) portal (data.rbi.org.in).

For any queries regarding data definitions or table content, users may contact the Department of Statistics and Information Management, Reserve Bank of India, at dbie@rbi.org.in.

Edition: April 2026
Supersedes: Comprehensive Guide 2017
Publication Platform: Database on Indian Economy (DBIE)

How to Use This Handbook

The RBI Bulletin presents key macroeconomic and financial statistics of the Indian economy in a structured tabular format. The tables included in the Bulletin are generated from the Reserve Bank’s central data repository (Centralised Information Management System, CIMS) to ensure consistency, standardisation, and reliability of published statistics.

Data Source and System Integration

All Bulletin tables are compiled using validated datasets maintained within the Reserve Bank’s data management systems. These datasets are derived from statutory returns submitted by regulated entities, operational systems of the Bank, data received from the Government and other official agencies, and International statistical reporting frameworks. The compilation process ensures alignment between published tables and the underlying time-series data disseminated through the Database on Indian Economy (DBIE) (https://data.rbi.org.in).

Availability of Long Time Series Data

While the Bulletin provides summary tables for the recent reference periods, the extended historical time series datasets underlying these tables are available through the Database on Indian Economy (DBIE). The DBIE allows users to access subject-wise datasets and download data in reusable formats.

Frequency of Data Updates

The tables in the Bulletin follow defined update frequencies, depending on the nature of the underlying data:

  • Daily (e.g., liquidity operations)

  • Weekly (e.g., RBI balance sheet indicators)

  • Fortnightly (e.g., monetary aggregates and banking indicators)

  • Monthly (e.g., price indices, trade statistics)

  • Quarterly (e.g., balance of payments, international investment position)

  • Annual / Financial Year-end (select indicators)

Each table reflects the reference period applicable to the dataset. Several summary tables may present indicators of different frequencies together for comparative reference.

Provisional and Final Data

Certain datasets published in the Bulletin may initially be marked as provisional, depending on the release practices of the source agency or reporting system. These are updated to final status as and when revisions are received from the source.

Data Consistency and Publication

The Reserve Bank follows established statistical standards and internal validation procedures to ensure accuracy, consistency and coherence across datasets published in the Bulletin and on DBIE.

Structure of Table Descriptions

Each table description in this Handbook follows a standard structure to ensure clarity and consistency in interpretation. The Coverage section outlines the dataset's scope and the economic indicators included. Data Presentation Features detail the frequency, measurement units, and key aspects of data presentation. The Notes section offers additional information on compilation methods, methodological considerations, institutional arrangements, or definitional clarifications to help ensure the data are understood correctly.

Data Compilation Framework

Data presented in the RBI Bulletin are generated from the Reserve Bank’s Data Warehouse through the Centralised Information Management System (CIMS), based on statutory returns, administrative data and information received from source agencies. Time-series data for all tables are available on the Database on Indian Economy (DBIE). Data are compiled from statutory returns (e.g., Form A, Form B), operational systems (e-Kuber, CCIL), and administrative reporting from Authorised Dealers and other regulated entities. Compilation broadly aligns with internationally accepted statistical standards where applicable (e.g., IMF BPM6 for BoP and IIP).

Disclaimer

While all efforts are made to ensure accuracy and consistency, data are subject to reporting constraints, revisions, and definitional changes over time. The interpretations, analyses, and conclusions drawn from the data are solely the responsibility of the users. The Reserve Bank of India is not responsible and shall not be liable for any loss, damage, or consequences arising from the use of the data or reliance placed on this Handbook.

Concepts, Definitions and Statistical Framework

This section outlines the key statistical concepts, classification principles and compilation frameworks used across the tables in this Handbook. Detailed methodological notes, where required, are provided in the respective table descriptions.

1. General Statistical Conventions

1.1 Reference Period

Data are presented as end-of-period values (e.g., reporting fortnight positions, month-end or quarter-end), period averages (e.g., financial year averages), or cumulative financial year totals, as applicable. Annual data for certain indicators may represent averages of monthly observations rather than end-of-period values.

1.2 Growth Rates

Growth rates generally represent year-on-year (Y-o-Y) changes, comparing the latest observation with the corresponding period of the previous year, unless otherwise specified. Monthly data are compared with the same month of the previous year, while quarterly data are compared with the corresponding quarter of the previous year.

1.3 Provisional and Final Data

Data may be provisional at the time of first release and are revised subsequently in accordance with the revision policy of the respective source agency.

1.4 Financial Year

The financial year in India runs from April to March.

1.5 Stock and Flow Data

Stock data refer to the position at a point in time (e.g., month-end or quarter-end). Flow data refer to transactions recorded over a period (e.g., cumulative financial year or quarterly flows). Most monetary and banking indicators represent stock positions, whereas indicators relating to trade, financial transactions and fiscal operations generally represent flow variables.

1.6 Base Year in Index Numbers

Many macroeconomic indicators, such as the Consumer Price Index (CPI), Wholesale Price Index (WPI), and Index of Industrial Production (IIP), are compiled as index numbers based on a specified base year. The base year serves as the benchmark period against which changes are measured, and index values indicate relative movements compared to the base year (set equal to 100).

1.7 Units and Rounding Conventions

Data are generally presented in ₹ crore, percentages, or index numbers (base = 100), as applicable. Minor differences in totals may arise due to rounding.

1.8 Data Frequency

Indicators are compiled at different frequencies depending on the source and reporting framework. Monetary and banking data are typically available at fortnightly or monthly frequency, price indices are compiled monthly, national accounts data are available quarterly and annually, while fiscal data are compiled on a monthly and annual basis.

2. National Accounts Concepts1

2.1. Gross Value Added (GVA) at Basic Prices

GVA at basic prices measures the value of output produced by a sector after deducting the value of intermediate consumption. It forms the production-side measure of economic activity. Sectoral GVA includes Agriculture, Industry and Services. GVA is compiled using the production approach in accordance with the System of National Accounts (SNA). Details on compilation methodology are published by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), Government of India.

2.2. Constant and Current Prices

  • Constant Prices: Adjusted for inflation using a specified base year.

  • Current Prices: Measured at prevailing market prices.

2.3. Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF)

Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF) represents the value of acquisition less disposal of fixed assets by resident producers during an accounting period. Fixed assets are those used repeatedly or continuously in production for more than one year. These include buildings and structures, machinery, and equipment, cultivated biological resources, and intellectual property products such as research and development and software.

2.4. Household Financial Savings (Net Financial Assets)

Net financial savings of households represent the difference between financial assets and financial liabilities during a period. It reflects the extent to which households are net providers of funds to the economy.

2.5. Household Financial Assets

Household financial assets include bank deposits, non-bank deposits, life insurance funds, currency holdings, mutual fund investments, pension funds and small savings instruments.

Household Sector. The household sector comprises individuals and unincorporated enterprises and represents a key source of financial savings in the economy.

2.6. Final Consumption Expenditure

Final consumption expenditure represents the total expenditure on goods and services by households and government for consumption purposes. It comprises private final consumption expenditure (PFCE) and government final consumption expenditure (GFCE).

2.7 GDP and GVA Relationship

Gross Domestic Product (GDP) at market prices is derived from GVA at basic prices by adding product taxes and subtracting product subsidies.

3. Monetary and Banking Concepts

3.1. Monetary Aggregates

Definition

Monetary aggregates refer to measures of money supply, representing liabilities of the banking system to the public, excluding inter-bank liabilities.

Measures

  • M1 (Narrow Money): Currency with the public + demand deposits + other deposits with RBI

  • M2: M1 + post office savings deposits

  • M3 (Broad Money): M1 + time deposits with banks

  • M4: M3 + total post office deposits

Sources of Money Supply (M3)

Money supply is derived from the consolidated balance sheet of the banking sector (RBI and commercial banks) and comprises:

  • Net bank credit to government

  • Bank credit to the commercial sector

  • Net foreign exchange assets

  • Government currency liabilities to the public

  • Adjusted for net non-monetary liabilities (as a balancing item)

Liquidity Aggregates

  • L1 = NM3 + Postal Deposits

  • L2 = L1 + Liabilities of Financial Institutions (term deposits, CDs, etc.)

  • L3 = L2 + Public Deposits with Non-banking Financial Companies

Liquidity aggregates (L1, L2 and L3) provide a broader measure of liquidity in the financial system by including, in addition to money supply, liabilities of financial institutions and non-banking financial entities. Liquidity aggregates are derived using NM3 as the base monetary aggregate. NM3 represents the residency-based broad money aggregate as recommended by WGMS.

3.2 Monetary Survey Concepts

Definition

The monetary survey presents a consolidated balance sheet of the banking sector, combining the Reserve Bank of India and the banking system, and provides the framework for analysing money supply.

Methodological Framework

The compilation of monetary aggregates and the Monetary Survey in India is based on the recommendations of the Working Group on Money Supply: Analytics and Methodology of Compilation (WGMS), chaired by Dr Y. V. Reddy (1998). The WGMS introduced refined monetary aggregates (NM1, NM2, NM3) based on the residency concept and an improved classification of the banking system's deposits and liabilities. Refined monetary aggregates are defined as follows:

NM1: Currency with the public + demand deposits + ‘other’ deposits with RBI

NM2: NM1 + short-term time deposits of residents (including certificates of deposit)

NM3: NM2 + long-term time deposits of residents + call/term funding from financial institutions

Components

The monetary survey presents:

  • Sources of money supply

  • Components of money supply

Key Aggregates

  • Monetary Survey: Consolidated balance sheet of RBI and banks

  • RBI Survey: Balance sheet of RBI showing sources and components of reserve money.

Key Concepts

  • RBI Credit to Banks: Lending by RBI to banks under liquidity facilities

  • RBI Credit to Commercial Sector: Direct credit extended by RBI to non-government entities

  • Net Non-Monetary Liabilities (RBI): Capital, reserves and other liabilities not included in monetary aggregates

  • Net Non-Monetary Liabilities (Banking System): Capital, reserves and other non-monetary liabilities of RBI and commercial banks

  • Domestic credit comprises net bank credit to government and bank credit to the commercial sector.

Government Currency Liabilities

Government currency liabilities comprise rupee coins and small coins issued by the Government of India and held by the public.

3.3 Reserve Money (M0)

Reserve money (M0), also known as base money, comprises:

  • Currency in circulation (notes and coins with the public and banks)

  • Bankers’ deposits with RBI

  • Other deposits with RBI

It represents the monetary liabilities of the Reserve Bank and forms the foundation for money supply expansion. On the sources side, reserve money is derived as the sum of net Reserve Bank credit to government, Reserve Bank credit to banks and the commercial sector, net foreign exchange assets and government currency liabilities to the public, adjusted for net non-monetary liabilities.

3.4 Components of Money Supply (M3)

  • Currency with the Public: Currency in circulation excluding cash held by banks

  • Notes in Circulation: Currency notes issued by RBI and held outside RBI

  • Circulation of Rupee Coin: Coins issued by Government of India held by the public

  • Circulation of Small Coins: Coins of denominations below one rupee

  • Cash on Hand with Banks: Currency held by banks for operational purposes

  • Deposit Money of the Public: Demand deposits held by the public with the banking system, including other deposits with RBI

  • Other Deposits with RBI: Deposits of foreign central banks, financial institutions and specified entities

  • Post Office Deposits: Savings, time and recurring deposits mobilised through post office schemes

3.5 Net Bank Credit to Government

Net bank credit to government includes RBI’s net credit to government and banks’ investment in government securities.

3.6 Reporting Fortnight

For banking and monetary statistics, a fortnight refers to the period from 1st to the 15th and from the 16th to the last day of the calendar month, both days inclusive. Statistical positions are generally reported as on the 15th and the last day of the month, in accordance with the Banking Laws (Amendment) Act, 2025. Earlier statistical series were compiled with reference to reporting Fridays; however, with effect from December 15, 2025, fortnightly data correspond to the mid-month (15th) and month-end positions.

3.7 Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL)

Net demand and time liabilities represent the total demand and time liabilities of banks, forming the base for CRR and SLR requirements.

  • Demand Liabilities: Payable on demand

  • Time Liabilities: Payable after a specified period

3.8 Deposits and Banking Liabilities

  • Deposits: Funds accepted by banks, repayable on demand or otherwise, including demand, savings and term deposits

  • Aggregate Deposits of Residents: Total deposits held by resident sectors with the banking system

  • Short-term Time Deposits: Deposits with maturity up to one year

  • Long-term Time Deposits: Deposits with maturity beyond one year

  • Inter-bank: Transactions between banks

  • Others: Deposits from non-bank entities including households, corporates and government

3.9 Bank Credit and Components

Definition

Bank credit refers to loans and advances extended by banks to various sectors of the economy.

Components

  • Loans (demand and term loans)

  • Cash credit

  • Overdrafts

  • Bills purchased and discounted

Classification

  • Domestic Credit: Credit extended to government and commercial sectors

  • Non-Food Credit: Non-food credit refers to total bank credit excluding credit extended for the procurement of food grains by public agencies such as FCI and State Governments.

  • Food Credit: Credit extended to agencies such as FCI and State Governments

Types of Facilities

  • Cash Credit: Working capital facility linked to inventory and receivables

  • Overdraft: Withdrawal beyond account balance up to a sanctioned limit

  • Bills Purchased/Discounted: Financing against trade bills

Gross Bank Credit: Total credit before provisions, write-offs or securitisation (aligned with BSR-1 framework)

Personal Loans: Personal Loans are loans extended to individuals for consumption purposes, such as housing, education, vehicles, and credit cards.

3.10 Investment Classification

Investment in Government Securities refers to banks’ holdings of central and state government securities, including those maintained to meet Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) requirements.

  • Government Securities: Investments in central and state government securities and treasury bills

  • SLR Securities: Approved securities held to meet SLR requirements

  • Non-SLR Securities: Corporate bonds, shares and other financial instruments

  • Commercial Paper: Unsecured short-term instrument issued by corporates

  • Equity Shares: Ownership instruments issued by corporates

  • Bonds and Debentures: Fixed-income instruments representing borrowings

  • Mutual Fund Units: Investments in pooled funds managed by asset management companies

3.11 Interbank and System Concepts

  • Liabilities to Banking System: Deposits and borrowings from other banks

  • Liabilities to Others: Deposits and borrowings from non-bank entities

  • Assets with Banking System: Balances and lending with other banks

  • Net Inter-bank Liabilities: Net obligations between banks

  • Other Demand and Time Liabilities (ODTL): Liabilities other than deposits

  • Credit to Primary Dealers: Lending to primary dealers

  • Money at Call and Short Notice: Short-term interbank funds

  • Call/Notice/Term Money: Classification based on maturity

3.12 RBI Balance Sheet Concepts

Structure

The Reserve Bank’s balance sheet comprises two broad segments:

  • Issue Department (currency issuance)

  • Banking Department (general banking and monetary operations)

Issue Department

  • Notes Issued: Total currency liabilities, comprising notes in circulation and notes held in the Banking Department

  • Assets of Issue Department: The Issue Department is responsible for currency issuance. Its liabilities comprise notes issued, including currency in circulation and notes held by the Banking Department. These liabilities are backed by eligible assets such as gold, foreign securities and rupee coins in accordance with the statutory provisions of the RBI Act, 1934.

Banking Department

Liabilities

  • Government Deposits: Balances maintained by the Central and State Governments with the RBI.

  • Bank Deposits: Bank deposits primarily represent balances maintained to meet Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) requirements and for settlement of interbank transactions.

  • Other Deposits: Deposits of financial institutions, foreign central banks and other entities

  • Other Liabilities: Contingency fund, asset development fund, revaluation accounts and other provisions

Assets

  • Foreign Currency Assets / Foreign Securities: Foreign currency assets include investments in foreign government securities, deposits with other central banks and international institutions, and are subject to valuation changes arising from exchange rate movements.

  • Investments: Holdings of government securities and other approved instruments

  • Loans and Advances: Credit extended to Central and State Governments, banks and other institutions

  • Bills Purchased and Discounted: Commercial bills acquired by RBI

  • Balances Held Abroad: Foreign currency balances maintained with foreign central banks and international institutions

  • Gold: Gold coin and bullion held as part of reserve assets

  • Other Assets: Fixed assets, accrued income, staff advances and miscellaneous assets

Key Concepts

  • Notes in Circulation: Currency notes issued by RBI and held by the public and banks, excluding those held within RBI

  • Notes held in Banking Department: Currency held by RBI for operational purposes

  • Total Liabilities or Assets: Balance sheet identity where total liabilities equal total assets

  • Claims on Government: Loans and investments of RBI in government securities

In the RBI survey framework, capital account and other items (net) act as balancing items, ensuring consistency between sources and components of reserve money.

Valuation and Revaluation Accounts

Certain balance sheet items are subject to periodic valuation. Changes in the value of foreign currency assets, gold and securities arising from exchange rate movements, gold prices and market yields are reflected through revaluation accounts such as the Currency and Gold Revaluation Account (CGRA) and Investment Revaluation Accounts, rather than being directly taken to the profit and loss account.

4. Rates and Ratios

4.1 Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)

The proportion of NDTL that scheduled commercial banks are required to maintain as cash balances with RBI. CRR requirements are governed under Section 42 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934.

4.2 Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)

The proportion of NDTL that banks must maintain in specified liquid assets, including government securities. SLR requirements are governed under Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

4.3 Credit-Deposit Ratio (CD Ratio)

The ratio of total bank credit (gross loans and advances) to total deposits of the banking system, expressed as a percentage. It indicates the extent to which deposits mobilised by banks are deployed in lending activities.

4.4 Incremental Credit-Deposit Ratio

Incremental Credit-Deposit Ratio is the ratio of the change in bank credit to the change in deposits over a specified period.

4.5 Investment-Deposit Ratio

Investment-Deposit Ratio is the ratio of total investments of banks to total deposits.

4.6 Incremental Investment-Deposit Ratio

Incremental Investment-Deposit Ratio is the ratio of the change in investments to the change in deposits over a specified period (ΔInvestments / ΔDeposits).

4.7 Cash-Deposit Ratio

Cash-Deposit Ratio is the ratio of cash balances maintained by banks to their total deposits.

4.8 Policy Repo Rate

Policy Repo Rate is the rate at which the Reserve Bank of India lends short-term funds to banks against government securities under the liquidity adjustment facility.

4.9 Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) Rate

Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) Rate is the rate at which the Reserve Bank absorbs liquidity from banks without collateral under the liquidity adjustment framework.

4.10 Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) Rate

The Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) Rate is the rate at which banks can borrow overnight funds from the Reserve Bank of India against approved securities in excess of their statutory liquidity ratio.

4.11 Base Rate

Base Rate is the minimum interest rate below which banks are not permitted to lend, except in specified cases, reflecting the cost of funds and operating expenses of banks.

4.12 Fixed Reverse Repo Rate

The rate at which banks deposit surplus funds with the Reserve Bank of India under the liquidity adjustment facility.

4.13 Bank Rate

Bank Rate is the rate at which the Reserve Bank of India is prepared to buy or rediscount bills of exchange or other commercial paper.

4.14 Marginal Cost of Funds-Based Lending Rate (MCLR)

MCLR is the minimum interest rate for lending determined by banks based on the marginal cost of funds, operating costs, and tenor premium.

4.15 Term Deposit Rate (>1 Year)

Term Deposit Rate refers to the interest rate offered by banks on deposits with maturity exceeding one year.

4.16 Savings Deposit Rate

Savings Deposit Rate is the interest rate paid by banks on balances maintained in savings accounts.

4.17 Call Money Rate (Weighted Average)

The Call Money Rate is the weighted average interest rate, based on transaction volumes, at which banks borrow and lend overnight funds in the interbank call money market.

5. Financial Market Concepts

5.1 Liquidity Management Framework

The Reserve Bank manages systemic liquidity through a corridor framework, with the policy repo rate as the operating target. The corridor is defined by the SDF rate as the floor and the MSF rate as the ceiling.

Key Instruments

  • Repo: Liquidity injection against eligible collateral

  • Reverse Repo: Liquidity absorption under the liquidity adjustment facility.

  • SDF: Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) serves as the floor of the liquidity corridor.

  • Marginal Standing Facility (MSF): Overnight borrowing facility above the policy repo rate

  • Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF): Framework for managing short-term liquidity

Liquidity Operations

  • Open Market Operations (OMO): Outright purchase or sale of government securities to inject or absorb durable liquidity

  • Variable Rate Repo: Auction-based liquidity injection at market-determined rates

  • Variable Rate Reverse Repo: Auction-based liquidity absorption through auctions

  • Standing Liquidity Facilities: On-demand liquidity support to eligible institutions, including MSF and refinance facilities.

  • Liquidity facilities for Primary Dealers (PDs) refer to funding support provided by the Reserve Bank to primary dealers to facilitate smooth functioning of the government securities market.

  • Net Liquidity Injection/Absorption: Net amount of liquidity injected into or absorbed from the banking system through various liquidity operations of the Reserve Bank. Net liquidity injection/absorption is computed as the sum of liquidity-providing operations (such as repo, MSF, OMO purchases) minus liquidity-absorbing operations (such as reverse repo, SDF, and OMO sales).

5.2 Money Market Instruments

Money market instruments are short-term instruments used for liquidity management.

  • Call Money: Overnight unsecured funds

  • Notice Money: Funds with maturity of 2–14 days

  • Term Money: Funds with maturity beyond 14 days up to one year

  • Commercial Paper (CP): Defined above

  • Certificates of Deposit (CD): Negotiable instruments issued by banks

These instruments are issued at market-determined interest rates and are reported in terms of outstanding amounts and issuance during the period.

5.3 Government Securities

Government securities represent borrowings of the Central and State Governments.

Instruments

  • Treasury Bills (T-Bills): Short-term instruments (91, 182, 364 days), issued at a discount and redeemed at face value. Treasury Bills are issued in standard maturities of 91-day, 182-day, and 364-day, along with 14-day intermediate Treasury Bills for state government cash management.

  • Treasury Bill Yield: Return determined through auction for short-term securities

  • 10-Year Government Security Yield: Benchmark long-term interest rate

Auction Mechanism

  • Competitive Bidding: Investors quote price or yield and are allotted securities based on cut-off

  • Non-Competitive Bidding: Investors receive allotment at weighted average price without quoting yield

  • Government securities and treasury bills are issued through both competitive and non-competitive bidding in auctions.

State Government Instruments

  • Auction Treasury Bills (ATBs): Treasury Bills issued by the Government of India and purchased by State Governments and other entities for investment of surplus funds.

Ownership of Government Securities

  • Ownership of government securities refers to the distribution of holdings of central and state government debt across different institutional sectors such as banks, insurance companies, provident and pension funds, mutual funds, foreign portfolio investors, the Reserve Bank of India, and others.

5.4 Yield Concepts

  • Cut-off Yield: Yield determined in auction

  • Coupon Yield: Annual coupon payment as a percentage of face value

  • Current Yield: Annual coupon payment as a percentage of market price

  • Yield to Maturity (YTM): Internal rate of return if the security is held till maturity

Securities may be issued through yield-based or price-based auctions.

The 10-year G-sec par yield (FBIL) represents the benchmark long-term sovereign yield published by Financial Benchmark India Pvt. Ltd. (FBIL), widely used as a reference rate for financial markets

5.5 Financial Resource Concepts

  • Financial resources are classified into bank and non-bank sources, and further into domestic and foreign sources.

  • Flow of Financial Resources: Incremental financing raised during a period from bank and non-bank sources.

  • Outstanding Credit: Stock of credit at a point in time

  • Net Basis Reporting: Data presented net of intermediation overlaps, except for equity and hybrid instruments which are shown on a gross basis

  • Hybrid Instruments (REITs/InvITs): Instruments combining features of equity and debt, including Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) and Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs)

  • Capital issues include public and rights issuances of equity shares and public issues of bonds and debentures.

5.6 Call/Term Funding

Call/term funding refers to borrowings by banks from financial institutions in call or term money markets.

Facility Limits and Utilisation

  • Limit: Maximum sanctioned amount under a facility

  • Outstanding: Actual utilisation of the facility at a point in time

5.7 Weighted Average Rate

Weighted average rate represents the average rate of transactions weighted by transaction value.

5.8 Annualised Forward Premia

Annualised forward premia measure the difference between forward and spot exchange rates expressed on an annualised basis.

Annualised Forward Premia(1-month)(%)=(Forward Premium/RBI Reference Rate)×100×12

Annualised Forward Premia (3-month)(%)=(Forward Premium/RBI Reference Rate)×100×4

Annualised Forward Premia (6-month)(%)=(Forward Premium / RBI Reference Rate)×100×2

Note: The reference rate of the last working day of the month is used for computation.

6. Government Finance Concepts

Government finance concepts relate to the receipts, expenditure, deficits and borrowing of the Central and State Governments.

6.1 Deficit Indicators

  • Revenue Deficit: Excess of revenue expenditure over revenue receipts

  • Fiscal Deficit: Excess of total expenditure over total receipts (i.e., revenue receipts and non-debt capital receipts), excluding borrowings

  • Primary Deficit: Fiscal deficit minus interest payments

6.2 Expenditure Classification

  • Developmental Expenditure: Expenditure on economic and social sectors such as infrastructure, health and education

  • Non-developmental Expenditure: Expenditure on interest payments, defence, administrative services and other committed liabilities

6.3 Receipts

  • Revenue Receipts: Tax and non-tax receipts that do not create liabilities

  • Capital Receipts: Receipts that create liabilities or reduce assets, including borrowings and disinvestment

6.4 Borrowing Concepts

  • Market Borrowings: Funds raised through issuance of government securities

  • Gross Borrowings: Total funds raised by the government through issuance of securities during a period.

  • Net Borrowings: Gross borrowings minus repayments

  • Financing of the fiscal deficit includes market borrowings, treasury bills, loans from financial institutions, and investments by insurance and pension funds.

6.5 State Government Finance

  • Ways and Means Advances (WMA): Short-term advances provided by RBI to meet temporary mismatches

  • Overdraft (OD): Borrowing beyond WMA limits, subject to regulatory conditions

  • Special Drawing Facility (SDF): Facility available against collateral such as government securities and reserve funds

6.6 Reserve Funds

  • Consolidated Sinking Fund (CSF): Fund maintained for future debt repayment

  • Guarantee Redemption Fund (GRF): Fund maintained to meet obligations arising from guarantees issued by State Governments

6.7 Other Concepts

  • Small Savings: Small savings represent household financial savings mobilised through government-backed schemes and constitute a source of non-market borrowing for the Government.

7. Payments and Settlements Systems

Payment and settlement systems facilitate the transfer of funds between entities and form a key component of financial market infrastructure. These systems are broadly classified into (i) payment system indicators, (ii) payment modes and channels, and (iii) payment system infrastructure.

7.1 Payment System Indicators

Payment system indicators capture transactions processed through settlement systems and payment systems, measured in terms of volume and value.

7.1.1 Settlement Systems (Financial Market Infrastructures – FMIs)

Settlement systems relate to financial market transactions and are primarily operated through centralised clearing infrastructure.

  • Government Securities Clearing: Settlement of outright, repo and tri-party repo transactions in government securities

  • Forex Clearing: Settlement of foreign exchange transactions

  • Rupee Derivatives: Settlement of interest rate and other rupee-denominated derivative transactions

7.1.2 Payment Systems

Payment systems include both large-value systems and retail payment systems.

(a) Large-value Payment System

  • RTGS (Real Time Gross Settlement): Real-time gross settlement of high-value interbank and customer transactions

(b) Retail Payment Systems

  • Retail payments comprise electronic and paper-based systems and are classified as follows:

Credit Transfers:

  • NEFT: Deferred net settlement system for retail payments

  • IMPS: Real-time interbank electronic fund transfer system

  • UPI: Instant real-time payment system using mobile platforms

  • AePS / APBS: Aadhaar-enabled payment systems for fund transfers and benefit payments

Debit Transfers and Direct Debits:

  • NACH (Debit): Electronic system for bulk and recurring debit transactions

  • BHIM Aadhaar Pay: Aadhaar-based merchant payment system

  • NETC: Electronic toll collection linked to bank accounts

Card Payments:

  • Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Payments at PoS terminals, online platforms and other acceptance channels.

Prepaid Payment Instruments (PPIs):

  • Wallets and Prepaid Cards: Stored-value instruments used for payments and fund transfers

Paper-based Instruments:

  • CTS (Cheque Truncation System): Electronic processing of cheques

7.2 Payment Modes and Channels

Payment modes and channels refer to the platforms through which transactions are initiated and executed.

7.2.1 Digital Channels

• Mobile Payments (App-based): Transactions carried out through mobile applications, including UPI and bank apps

Classified into:

  • Intra-bank transactions (within the same bank)

  • Inter-bank transactions (across banks)

• Internet Banking: Transactions executed through net banking platforms

Classified into:

  • Intra-bank

  • Inter-bank

7.2.2 Cash Access and Withdrawal Channels

These relate to physical or assisted access points and are classified by instrument type

  • ATMs: Cash withdrawals using Credit cards, Debit cards and Prepaid cards

  • PoS Terminals: Cash withdrawal using debit cards and prepaid cards

  • Micro-ATMs (AePS): Aadhaar-enabled cash withdrawal and basic banking services

7.3 Payment System Infrastructure

Payment system infrastructure represents the physical and digital infrastructure and acceptance infrastructure supporting payment systems. This includes:

• Cards:

  • Credit cards

  • Debit cards

• Prepaid Payment Instruments (PPIs):

  • Wallets

  • Prepaid cards

• ATMs:

  • Bank-owned ATMs

  • White Label ATMs (WLAs)

• Micro-ATMs

• Point of Sale (PoS) Terminals

• QR Code Infrastructure:

  • Bharat QR

  • UPI QR

8. Price and Production Indices

Inflation measures track changes in the general price level over time and are key indicators of price stability in the economy.

8.1 Consumer Price Index (CPI)

Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures changes in retail prices of a representative basket of goods and services consumed by households. It reflects the cost of living and is used for monetary policy assessment. CPI (Combined) is compiled and released by the National Statistical Office (NSO), MoSPI.

Coverage

  • Rural, Urban and Combined indices

  • Multiple consumption categories such as food, housing, transport and services

Measurement

CPI inflation is generally measured on a year-on-year (Y-o-Y) basis.

8.2 Wholesale Price Index (WPI)

Wholesale Price Index (WPI) measures changes in prices of goods at the wholesale level before reaching the retail market. It reflects price movements in production and supply chains.

Components

  • Primary Articles (food and non-food)

  • Fuel and Power

  • Manufactured Products

WPI is compiled and released by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce and Industry.

8.3 Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW)

CPI-IW measures changes in prices of a basket of goods and services consumed by industrial workers and is compiled by the Labour Bureau, Government of India.

Other consumer price indices include the CPI for Agricultural Labourers (CPI-AL) and the CPI for Rural Labourers (CPI-RL), compiled by the Labour Bureau, each with a separate base year.

8.4. Index of Industrial Production (IIP)

The Index of Industrial Production (IIP) measures changes in the volume of industrial output over time relative to a base year, covering mining, manufacturing and electricity sectors.

9. External Sector Concepts

9.1 Balance of Payments (BoP)

Balance of Payments is a systematic record of economic transactions between residents and non-residents, comprising: Current Account, Capital Account, Financial Account as per BPM6.

9.2 Foreign Exchange Reserves

Foreign exchange reserves are held and managed by the Reserve Bank of India. Foreign exchange reserves comprise Foreign Currency Assets, Gold, Special Drawing Rights (SDR), and the Reserve Tranche Position in the IMF. Changes in foreign exchange reserves reflect not only transactions but also valuation effects due to exchange rate movements of non-US currencies.

9.3 Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)

FDI refers to investment reflecting a lasting interest and control in an enterprise.

9.4 Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI)

FPI refers to Investment in financial securities without management control.

9.5 Non-Resident Deposits

Non-resident deposits refer to deposits held in India by non-residents with banks, denominated in domestic or foreign currency. Non-resident deposits include FCNR(B), NRE and NRO deposit schemes.

9.6 Debit–Credit Convention in Balance of Payments

In the BoP, an increase in assets or a decrease in liabilities is recorded as a debit. An increase in liabilities or a decrease in assets is recorded as a credit.

9.7 Errors and Omissions

Errors and omissions represent the statistical balancing item in the balance of payments.

Trade and Exchange Rate Concepts

9.8 Exchange Rate (INR per Foreign Currency)

The exchange rate represents the value of the Indian Rupee in terms of a foreign currency, expressed as units of Rupees per unit of foreign currency.

In addition to market-determined exchange rates, the Reserve Bank publishes reference rates for select major currencies.

Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rate (NEER/REER) indices measure the value of the domestic currency against a basket of currencies, with REER adjusted for inflation differentials.

9.9 RBI Reference Rate

It represents the daily indicative exchange rate published by the Reserve Bank for major foreign currencies such as USD and Euro.

9.10 Forward Premia

Forward Premia represent the difference between forward and spot exchange rates, expressed as an annualised percentage of the spot rate.

9.11 Imports

Imports refer to the value of goods and services purchased by residents from non-residents during a specified period.

9.12 Exports

Exports refer to the value of goods and services supplied by residents to non-residents during a specified period.

9.13 Trade Balance

Trade Balance represents the difference between exports and imports of goods and services. Trade data are often classified into oil and non-oil components for analytical purposes.

RBI Foreign Exchange Operations

9.14 Gross Purchase / Gross Sale:

  • Gross Purchase: Total foreign currency purchased by the Reserve Bank

  • Gross Sale: Total foreign currency sold by the Reserve Bank

9.15 Net Purchase / Sale of Foreign Currency

Net Purchase/Sale of Foreign Currency represents the net amount of foreign exchange bought or sold by the Reserve Bank in the foreign exchange market during a specified period. ₹ equivalent at contract rate represents the domestic currency value of foreign exchange transactions converted at the agreed transaction exchange rate.

Cumulative Purchase/Sale: Cumulative purchase/sale (over end-March) represents the aggregate net foreign exchange operations of the Reserve Bank from the beginning of the financial year up to the reporting period.

9.16 Outstanding Net Forward Sales / Purchase

Outstanding Net Forward Sales/Purchase represent the net forward foreign exchange commitments of the Reserve Bank at the end of the period.

Derivatives and Forward Market Concepts

9.17 Currency Futures (segment)

Currency Futures represent exchange-traded derivative contracts to buy or sell foreign currency at a future date at a predetermined price.

9.18 Forward Contracts

Forward contracts are agreements to buy or sell foreign currency at a specified future date and are classified by residual maturity and position (long or short).

Long / Short Position:

  • Long Position: Commitment to purchase foreign currency in future

  • Short Position: Commitment to sell foreign currency in future

9.19 Residual maturity

Residual maturity refers to the remaining time to maturity of a forward contract from the reporting date.

Maturity Classification

Forward contracts are classified into maturity buckets (e.g., up to 1 month, 1–3 months, 3–12 months, and above 1 year) based on residual maturity for analytical and reporting purposes.

External Position Indicators

9.20 Export Credit Refinance (ECR)

Export Credit Refinance (ECR) was a facility provided by the Reserve Bank to banks to refinance export credit extended to exporters (now phased out and merged with system liquidity).

9.21 Gross Foreign Assets

Gross Foreign Assets represent total foreign assets before adjusting for foreign liabilities.

9.22 International Investment Position (IIP)

IIP refers to the stock of external financial assets and liabilities of a country at a point in time. Net IIP represents the difference between external assets and liabilities.

9.23 Residence Principle

External sector statistics follow the residence concept; whereby institutional units are classified based on their centre of predominant economic interest.

9.24 BPM6

BPM6 refers to the sixth edition of the IMF Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual.

This table presents the Monetary Survey, which is the consolidated balance sheet of the banking system used to analyse money supply. The Monetary Survey provides the analytical framework linking money supply (M3/NM3) to its components and sources. It provides:

  • Monetary Aggregates NM1, NM2, and NM3

  • Components of Money Supply, including currency with the public, deposits of residents and ‘other’ deposits with RBI.

  • Sources of Money Supply, including domestic credit, government liabilities, net foreign exchange assets, capital account and other items (net) - represents the balancing item in the monetary survey framework.

  • The table integrates RBI and banking-sector balance sheet data.

3. Data Presentation Features

  • Figures relate to reporting fortnights and March-end position.

  • Based on consolidated balance sheet approach.

  • Monetary aggregates are derived using defined accounting identities.

4. Notes

  • NM1 = Currency with the Public + Demand Deposits + ‘Other’ Deposits with RBI.

  • NM2 = NM1 + Short-term Time Deposits.

  • NM3 is derived from its components as well as its sources identity. On the components side, NM3 = NM2 + Long-term Time Deposits + Call/Term Funding from Financial Institutions. On the sources side, NM3 = Domestic Credit + Government’s Currency Liabilities to the Public + Net Foreign Exchange Assets − Capital Account − Other Items (Net). NM2 and NM3 aggregates exclude FCNR(B) deposits.

  • Compilation follows the methodology of the Working Group on Money Supply (WGMS).

  • Classification is based on the residency principle. Complementary to Tables 6 and 7.

OD is availed by State Governments beyond their WMA limits, subject to regulatory conditions.

  • Average amount availed represents total accommodation (SDF/WMA/OD) divided by the number of days for which the facility was utilised during the month.

item.title: Urban Consumer Confidence Survey
item.description:
Today, the Reserve Bank released the results of September 2026 round of its bi-monthly urban consumer confidence survey (UCCS)1. The survey collects current perceptions (vis-à-vis a year ago) and one year ahead expectations of households on general economic situation, employment scenario, overall price situation, own income and spending. The survey was conducted during September 10-20, 2026, covering 6,054 respondents across 19 major cities.

Highlights:

  1. Households’ confidence for the current period moved marginally with the Current Situation Index (CSI)2 at 87.9 from 88.3 in the previous round (Chart 1).

  2. Consumer optimism for the year ahead remained in positive terrain, albeit with slight moderation in the Future Expectations Index (FEI) (Chart 1).

  3. The consumer sentiments are optimistic on income and spending amid some concerns regarding economic situation, employment and prices going forward (Tables 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6).

item.title: Bank Lending Survey for Q2:2026-27
item.description:
Today, the Reserve Bank released the results of 37th round of its Bank Lending Survey (BLS)1, which captures qualitative assessment and expectations of major scheduled commercial banks (SCBs) on credit parameters (viz., loan demand as well as terms and conditions of loans) for major economic sectors2. The latest round of the survey, which was conducted during Q2:2026-27, collected senior loan officers’ assessment of credit parameters for Q2:2026-27 and their expectations for Q3 and Q4:2026-27 and Q1:2027-28.

Highlights:

A.Assessment for Q2:2026-27

  • Bankers reported improved optimism in credit demand across major sectors of the economy during Q2:2026-27 (Chart 1 and Table 1).

  • Bankers indicated some easing in loan terms and conditions at the aggregate level (Table 2).

B. Expectations for Q3:2026-27

  • Bankers’ expectations on loan demand improved across sectors (except for agriculture sector) in Q3:2026-27 majorly driven by seasonal demand.

  • Overall loan terms and conditions are expected to remain unchanged during Q3:2026-27 over previous quarter (Table 1 and 2).

C. Expectations for Q4:2026-27 and Q1:2027-28

  • Going forward, bankers’ expectations on loan demand exhibited sustained optimism in upcoming quarters (Table 3).

The weights of +1.0, 0.5, 0, -0.5 and -1.0 are assigned for computing NR from aggregate per cent responses on 5-point scale, i.e., substantial increase/ considerable easing, moderate increase/ somewhat easing, no change, moderate decrease/ somewhat tightening, substantial decrease/ considerable tightening for loan demand/loan terms and conditions parameters respectively. NR ranges between -100 to 100. Any value greater than zero indicates expansion/optimism and any value less than zero indicates contraction/pessimism. Increase in loan demand is considered optimism (Table 1), while for loan terms and conditions, a positive value of net response indicates easy terms and conditions (Table 2).
